finding elusive, tiny plant-eaters. Conservationists in the Siebers Experimental Forest discovered not one, but 20 spotted seed bugs feeding in a greenhouse, in about one square foot. Only 80 seed beetles remain spawning in the brook outwells, said Jean Sauvage, the forest superintendent. Brantton Guggenheizen, a geneticist with the forest, and her team investigate the loss of native plant species around the reservoir and installed an insect-monitoring system last spring in the 4.5 acre Siebers Forest, now being restored off Mazeppa Drive. The network of robotic alerts and solar-powered sensors emit infrared pulses to attract rare and elusive native plants. The devices interpret light, temperature, and heat to track bedbugs, stinkbugs and often their prey. Environmental scientists monitoring the wildlife species ongoing conservation program set up 12 camera trails transecting the watershed. Scientists at the wildlife sanctuary hope the system will provide them with a real-time tracking tool as they begin to decipher the life histories of the plant species within this redoubt of eastern Newfoundland. A camera set up on an eastward forest trail facing the west could see the life patterns of an entire cohort of migrating insects. "Assuming our sensors detect a mature mating male fruit fly along with the pheromones he produces, we'd be able to track the mated female across the desert without being looking for her the whole time. If we take an even broader view, we'd be able to reconstruct the synchronous flowering and pollination events in the desert, which could be of use for conservationists, farmers and ecologists," said biologist Dr. Arthur Farrington, who is leading the project. The team at Siebers Forest operates from a lab, complete with rye fields, greenhouses and water collection operations. Over the next week, staff on site plan to take photos of rare and sensitive vegetation species under ecological stress to pinpoint which of the native species have found long-term survival in the relentless light of intense artificial illumination. Rather than using chemicals to manage the pests creating stress on natural forests, conservationists are using benign and selective, pressure-free methods to address ecological problems, and work to prevent destructive energy generation such as inadequate solar or wind facilities, the scientists said. The employees at Siebers Forest use computer networked remote monitoring of the forest to measure light down to the millimeter, advance weather forensics, and drive specialized pilot planes fitted with high-resolution imagers to fly automated, high accuracy measurements of ground, cloud and water vapor conditions with extended setups that can capture images with the same retention precision as the human eye.
